The Coalsack Nebula (Southern Coalsack, or simply the Coalsack) is a dark nebula, which is visible to the naked eye as a dark patch obscuring part of the Milky Way east of Acrux (Alpha Crucis) in the constellation of Crux.
The Coalsack Nebula covers nearly 7° by 5° and extends into the neighboring constellations Centaurus and Musca. The first observation by a European was reported by Vicente Yáñez Pinzón in 1499. It was named "il Canopo fosco" (the dark Canopus) by Amerigo Vespucci and was also called "Macula Magellani" (Magellan's Spot) or "Black Magellanic Cloud" in opposition to the Magellanic Clouds.

The Coalsack is traditionally recognized as a dark constellation by many cultures.
Historically any other dark cloud in the night sky was called a "coalsack". Richard Hinckley Allen in 1899 called a different dark nebula in Cygnus the Northern Coalsack.
In Australian Aboriginal astronomy, the Coalsack forms the head of the emu in the sky in several Aboriginal cultures.

The Horsehead Nebula (also known as Barnard 33 or B33) is a small dark nebula located about 1,375 light-years (422 pc) from Earth in the constellation of Orion. The nebula is located just to the south of Alnitak, the easternmost star of Orion's Belt, and is part of the much larger Orion molecular cloud complex. It appears within the southern region of the dense dust cloud known as Lynds 1630, along the edge of the much larger, active star-forming H II region called IC 434. It is one of the most identifiable nebulae because of its resemblance to a horse's head.
The nebula was discovered by Williamina Fleming in 1888 on a photographic plate taken at the Harvard College Observatory. One of the first descriptions was made by E. E. Barnard, describing it as: "Dark mass, diam. 4′, on nebulous strip extending south from ζ Orionis", cataloguing the dark nebula as Barnard 33.
It has an easily recognizable shape which resembles the head of a horse.
